notes: 'spirit-dessert' and 'hot-dessert' below are duplicated (cross-referenced) from spirit_pairings.json and coffee_pairings.json respectively, because both RULES entries are gated on d.course === 'DESSERT' and this file is meant to collect every dessert-facing pairing rule in one place, regardless of which beverage family it belongs to.

'dessert-course-food' captures the generic foodPairClauseFor() DESSERT branch in hospitalityKnowledge.js, which is a food+food (not food+drink) clause used when a dessert is paired against a main/source dish with no wine anchor.

entries.principle: a spirit is the natural way to close the meal once dessert is finished
entries.rotation: deterministic-hash (single-variant clause set, no rotation needed)

professional: A spirit like this is a natural way to close the meal after dessert.
friendly: A neat pour like that is honestly the perfect way to finish once the dessert's done.
luxury: A spirit of this weight is the natural way to close the evening once the dessert is finished.

entries.principle: classic way to finish a meal: a hot drink alongside dessert
entries.rotation: deterministic-hash (single-variant clause set, no rotation needed)

professional: A hot drink alongside dessert is the classic way to finish the meal.
friendly: A coffee with dessert is the classic move, always works.
luxury: A hot pour alongside dessert is the traditional, and still the best, way to close the meal.

entries.principle: light-vs-indulgent framing based on the dessert's own richness tag

phrases.friendly_or_professional_light: Keeps things light rather than heavy after the {sourceName}.
phrases.friendly_or_professional_indulgent: A properly sweet way to close things out after the {sourceName}.

template_vars.sourceName: lowercased name of the source/main dish being closed out

entries.fidelity_note: foodPairClauseFor() only has ONE phrasing per branch (no professional/friendly/luxury split for course===DESSERT specifically, unlike the STARTER branch which does split by tone) -- copied verbatim, not invented.

entries.source: aiService.js addPerfectPairings() pairingRules["Sweet finish pairing"] (DRINK typedPair)
entries.recommended_style: irish coffee, espresso, whisky, or cognac
entries.principle: classic dessert-closing drinks spanning both hot-drink and spirit families (candidate-generation rule, not a narrative phrase rule)
entries.label: Sweet finish pairing
entries.fidelity_note: Keyword candidate generator (pickVariedMenuItem against type DRINK), no professional/friendly/luxury phrase variants in source; this rule has no companion 'MAIN'/food typedPair (dessert is the anchor dish itself, not a side).

dessert_narrative_classification.description: Used when composing a dessert recommendation that references BOTH the main dish already ordered AND a wine already in the cart -- the 'light vs indulgent' framing decision.
dessert_narrative_classification.applies_when: target.categoryType === 'DESSERT' && source (anchor dish) present && cartWine present

classification_logic.fallback_regex: /lemon|sorbet|fruit|berry/i tested against the dessert item's own name, used ONLY when richness is not a finite number (i.e. the item has no richness tag)

templates.light: {dessertName} keeps things light rather than heavy after the {sourceName}.
templates.indulgent: {dessertName} is a properly rich way to close out the {sourceName} and {cartWineName}.
